newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks close lower as profit-taking persists.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks close lower as profit-taking persists.

text.p: Persistent profit-taking in response to recent sharp gains sent South Korean stocks to a lower close after Saturday's half-day session, brokers said.
Industrial unrest over a new labour law, that has hit South Korea for more than three weeks, continued to be ignored as a major factor in the market, they said.
The composite index ended the session at 694.23, down 0.99 percent or 6.95 points on the day.
"Declines were nearly across the board as impatient investors preferred to cash in their gains," said Koh Kyung-bae of Hyundai Securities.
Main gainers were small- to medium-capitalised stocks perceived to be undervalued.
Blue chips also fell across the board, with Korea Electric Power Corp an exception. The electricity monopoly closed flat at 28,600, with its shares actively trading.
Brokers said Korea Electric was a favourite of foreign investors.
On Saturday, a union umbrella group spearheading wildcat strikes said it would call off stoppages from Monday and instead would hold strikes once a week.
The strikes erupted in protest at the forced passage on December 26 of the new labour bill that allows worker layoffs and the replacement of striking workers.
"The labour strikes have already been reflected on the stock market. It will have no further impact if there is no dramatic development," said Koh Kyung-bae of Hyundai Securities.
The government has said the wildcat strikes could make it hard for the nation to control the snowballing trade deficit.
The Bank of Korea earlier said this year's trade deficit was forecast to narrow to around $15 billion from a provisional $20 billion shortfall for 1996. --YOO CHOON-SIK (822) 727 5646
